summary: Defines and tests a fuller, trusted account of every student’s learning, bringing the authoritative academic record into a clear relationship with capabilities, recognised experiences, microcredentials and student evidence so students can credibly articulate what they know, can do and contribute.
detailSummary:
King’s can give students a fuller account of their learning than modules, marks and degree classification alone can provide, but the final container should not be predetermined. The authoritative academic transcript may remain one trusted layer within a broader educational record or portfolio that also brings together capabilities, recognised experiences, institutional microcredentials and evidence contributed by the student.

The central design problem is trust. Students should be able to see where knowledge and capabilities came from and understand the status of what they are looking at: what King’s has certified or formally recognised, what the student can evidence and what remains a student claim. Discovery will therefore define the trust and authority model, policy principles and information architecture before the university decides whether the eventual experience should be an enhanced transcript, a broader portfolio containing the transcript, a successor to the HEAR or a combination.

King’s will then test candidate models with willing trailblazer programmes, faculties and relevant professional services using real student journeys and evidence. The aim is to build operational and academic capability deeply enough to expose what formal recognition actually requires, then test whether successful models travel beyond highly committed settings before institutionalising them.

The Digital Student Experience Hub will deliver the eventual digital capability against the vision, trust model, information architecture and requirements established here. King’s Edge will not build a separate record platform. Responsibly governed aggregate insight may also give programmes, faculties and King’s a richer account of the knowledge and capabilities its education develops.
problemSolved: The academic transcript records modules, marks and classification but does not make visible the fuller knowledge, capabilities and recognised learning students develop through their course and broader King’s experience. Students are left to identify, evidence and communicate much of that value themselves, while King’s lacks an agreed trust architecture for bringing richer forms of learning into relationship with its authoritative academic record.
whatChanges: Every student can access a fuller and trusted account of their learning in which the authoritative academic record, recognised achievements, capabilities and student evidence are clearly related without blurring their status. King’s settles the record or portfolio architecture through discovery and trailblazer evidence, then institutionalises the model that preserves both student usefulness and institutional trust.

caseForChange.problem:
The academic transcript provides an authoritative record of modules, marks and classification, but the knowledge and capabilities developed through a course remain largely buried within those outcomes. Learning arising through students’ broader experience of learning and development can be occluded from the formal record altogether.

Students are therefore left to identify, evidence and translate much of the value of their education for themselves. Those with greater confidence, networks or familiarity with professional language are better placed to build a compelling account of what they have learned and can contribute.

Simply adding more information to the academic transcript does not solve the problem. Different kinds of statement carry different authority. A student may claim a capability, provide credible evidence of it, complete recognised learning or hold an achievement King’s is prepared to certify. Combining these without a clear trust model risks weakening confidence in the authoritative record.

King’s also does not yet have a sufficiently rich and connected view of the capabilities and recognised learning developed across its students. This limits its ability to demonstrate the collective relevance and value of its education to the wider world.
caseForChange.opportunity:
King’s can create a fuller trusted educational record in which the authoritative academic transcript sits in a clear relationship with capabilities, recognised experiences, institutional microcredentials and student-contributed evidence. The first opportunity is to define the trust and authority model rather than choose a container too early.

Discovery can establish the distinctions between certified, formally recognised, evidenced and claimed learning; the academic and policy rules that should govern each; and the information model needed to carry provenance and status visibly. Competing service concepts can then be prototyped, including an enriched transcript, a broader portfolio containing the transcript, an evolving educational record during study and different completion records.

Willing trailblazer partners can test the strongest models with real students and real evidence, building the academic, Registry and operational capability needed to make richer recognition credible. This allows King’s to learn what can be governed and delivered in practice rather than only what looks coherent on paper. Portability testing can then distinguish what should become institutional from arrangements that depend on unusual local effort or context.

Students can ultimately draw on a trusted record during study and transition to communicate a distinctive account of what they know, can do and contribute. Responsibly aggregated insight can also give King’s a stronger view of the capabilities its education develops and a richer basis for demonstrating relevance to the wider world.
caseForChange.whyNow:
For much of the recent past, a degree title and classification could operate as sufficient shorthand for a graduate’s capabilities and future potential. That assumption is weakening as graduate pathways change, AI reshapes work and government, business and students scrutinise more closely what degree-level education enables people to know, do and contribute.

Connected work on student purpose, a shared skills language, recognised learning and institutional microcredentials now creates the possibility of a much fuller account of learning. But those elements should not simply be accumulated in one interface without resolving the authority attached to each.

The Digital Student Experience Hub creates a live delivery window in which record, evidence and recognition capabilities can eventually be integrated into the mainstream student experience. That makes it important to define the trust and information architecture now, while deliberately holding back from institutional implementation until discovery and trailblazer work show what is credible and portable.
caseForChange.intendedChange:
King’s establishes a fuller, trusted and evolving account of every student’s learning. The authoritative academic record remains clear, while students can also see and use relevant capabilities, recognised experiences, institutional microcredentials and their own evidence with the status and provenance of each made explicit.

Available during study as well as at completion, the experience helps students reflect on what they are developing and communicate what they know, can do and contribute. King’s gains a connected and responsibly aggregated view of the capabilities and recognised learning its education develops.

The final record or portfolio architecture is determined through discovery, deep trailblazer use and portability testing rather than prespecified as an enhanced transcript. The Digital Student Experience Hub delivers the enduring digital service against the agreed trust model, information architecture and institutional requirements.
